issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a male torture survivor, sexual-trauma-specific verbal cues are possible only if sexual torture or sexual humiliation is part of the trauma, but the rest of the profile provides no corresponding sexual content in memory, appraisals, threat, or coping. As selected, this trigger appears disconnected from the trauma representation and is hard to justify clinically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him implies shame/marked visible contamination or exposure. That could occur after torture, but here it is not supported by the memory items, trigger content, or other appraisals, making it feel mismatched with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is poorly linked to the active formulation. The main connected pattern is triggers ↔ negative appraisals with memory-linked re-experiencing and threat-driven compliance/detachment. Gambling introduces a separate excitement-seeking coping style that is not reflected elsewhere and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette:
At 70, Rafael Morales came to treatment after years of insisting that what happened to him belonged to another life and another country. He is a widowed Latino man who still works as a welder, and for decades he had organized himself around long hours, routine, and silence. When he first began to speak about the trauma, his account broke apart in the middle. He would start with one detail, stop suddenly, stare at the floor, and say that once he tried to explain it, he lost the thread and could not finish. Even so, certain moments were unmistakably vivid. He described being taken and tortured by armed men, held in a confined space where there was nowhere to move and no way out. He remembered the absolute certainty of having no options, the sense that every sound might mean another assault was about to begin. Above all he remembered gunshots nearby and episodes of direct violence, each one arriving without warning. In his telling, the terror was mixed with humiliation and helplessness, and he had come to believe that what happened was tied to the way he acted in those moments. He said he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened.

In the years after, Rafael did not speak about the torture in any sustained way. When memories surfaced, he detached from them as if he were stepping sideways out of his own life. He tried hard not to think about the trauma at all. If an image or sensation pushed through, he would shut it down, go numb, or busy his hands with work until the feeling passed. Yet the memories did not feel like old memories. What frightened him was how quickly the past became present. A sharp sound could collapse time. A gunshot on television, a car backfiring in the street, even metal striking metal in the shop in the wrong rhythm could make him feel, for a few moments, as if he were back in that room with armed men nearby. His body reacted before he could remind himself where he was. He knew he was in his welding bay, mask in hand, but the memory arrived with such force that it felt like something happening now, not something over.

The shop became one of the places where this was most obvious. Welding is noisy, full of bursts, bangs, and threat-like sounds, and Rafael had learned the layout carefully so he could keep himself from feeling cornered. If another worker blocked the narrow passage beside his station, or if equipment was stacked in a way that left him with no easy path out, he felt a surge of alarm he could not easily explain. He would quietly reposition things, step away, or volunteer to work in a different area rather than remain in a spot that felt closed in. He did not tell coworkers why. Instead, when he felt threatened or pressured, he became overly agreeable. He said yes too quickly, apologized even when he had done nothing wrong, and let other men choose the assignments. To others he could appear easygoing, but from his perspective compliance felt safer than risking conflict with anyone who might turn dangerous. He was certain that you can never know who will harm you.

Rafael has been widowed for some years, and the loss left him with fewer places to speak freely. His restraint hardened into habit. Family members noticed that if conversation turned toward political violence, crime, or stories of abuse, he either left the room or went flat and distant. On the rare occasions he tried to tell more of what happened, the effort often ended in anger. He would begin haltingly, then his face tightened and his voice rose; the memory brought intense rage, so strong that he sometimes had to stop for fear of what would come out of him. That rage coexisted with blame directed inward. He replayed his own actions during the torture and judged them mercilessly, as though there had been something decisive he failed to do. In his mind, other people remained unpredictable and dangerous, while he remained the man who had not acted correctly when it mattered most.

What finally brought Rafael to seek help was not a single crisis but an accumulation of moments he could no longer dismiss. Recently, after a loud bang at work, he froze and then found himself trembling with fury and shame, unable to return to his station for the rest of the shift. He told his supervisor only that he felt unwell. At home that evening he realized how small his life had become, arranged around avoiding certain sounds, certain conversations, certain positions in a room. He said he was tired of the past arriving “like it is still happening,” and tired of feeling that danger could come from anyone at any time. Still, even in asking for help, Rafael was wary. What he feared most was being overwhelmed by the memories or judged for what he did and did not do. What he hoped for, stated cautiously, was to be able to talk without losing the thread and to stand in his own life without feeling trapped.
